newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan foreign minister to tackle China, U.S. ties.
newsitem.headline: Japan foreign minister to tackle China, U.S. ties.

text.p: Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda was one of only two cabinet members retained by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in his new government formed on Thursday, mainly because of a busy foreign policy schedule.
"We must further develop ties with the United States," Ikeda told a news conference after being re-appointed to his post. "I would especially emphasise the importance of Okinawa.

"We must also improve ties with China on the whole, although there are some different positions our two countries take," said Ikeda, a former Finance Ministry bureaucrat and son-in-law of the late prime minister Hayato Ikeda.
Ikeda's first task is to tackle the thorny issue of disputed islands with Russia, an issue which has prevented the two countries from signing a World War Two peace treaty.
Ikeda will meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov when he arrives in Tokyo on November 14.
The main item on the agenda is the question of Russian-held islands off northern Japan, called Southern Kuriles by Moscow and Northern Territories by Japan.
Ikeda must toe a delicate line because any concessions to the Russians could be misinterpreted by China and South Korea, which are also embroiled in territorial disputes with Japan.

Ikeda then travels to Manila the following week for a ministerial meeting of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, where he is expected to meet Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.

Foreign Ministry officials said Sino-Japanese ties have hit rock bottom since they were normalised in 1978 because of a heated row over Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea. Called Senkakus in Japanese and Diaoyus in Chinese, the islands are also claimed by China and Taiwan.
The issue erupted in anti-Japanese demonstrations in Hong Kong in September after the death of a pro-China Hong Kong activist during protests near the islands.
China has also used some harsh words against Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's visit to the controversial Yasukuni Shrine in Tokyo in July.

Hashimoto became the first Japanese leader in a decade to pay homage to the place of worship enshrining Japan's 2.6 million war dead since the 19th century, including Class-A war criminals such as wartime premier General Hideki Tojo.

It remained to be seen whether Ikeda can mend fences with Qian and pave the way for a private meeting between Hashimoto and Chinese President Jiang Zemin, both of whom are to attend the APEC summit at Subic Bay on November 25.
In Manila, Ikeda may also meet new South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha, appointed just this week.
South Korea and Japan are engaged in another bitter row over two disputed South Korean-held islands in the Sea of Japan.
With Christopher, Ikeda has the daunting task of smoothly drafting a set of new military cooperation guidelines under the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty.

Ikeda must also seek an agreement with Washington in details of an announced plan to cut back on U.S. military bases on southern Okinawa, where public anger flared last year over the concentration of military facilities there.
